paras: The expulsion of Black residents from Webrum, Pennsylvania, took place on February 23, 1903, when white residents of the town pulled down the shacks of its Black residents with ropes and poles and drove out about twenty people. It followed a shooting about ten days earlier in which a Black man, Sterling Aiken, was reported to have wounded a white bookkeeper and escaped. The displaced residents left on a freight train for Vintondale, and Southern papers reprinted the wire story as evidence that the North treated Black people no better than the South.

According to a dispatch datelined Indiana, Pa., February 24, Sterling Aiken, described as "a negro," had shot Welton Thomas, "a bookkeeper of Webrum," ten days earlier and then escaped. Webrum residents then ordered all the Black people in the town, about twenty, to leave the neighborhood. The longer version of the dispatch said they were given several days' notice to quit and later warnings, all of which went unheeded, and it described the whole affair as "a race war which broke out ten days ago."

On February 23, after the Black residents had not left, white residents attacked their quarters with ropes and poles. In the fuller account, "a white mob" marched on the quarters, rigged tackle on the shacks and pulled on the ropes until the structures were in ruins. The short dispatch spoke of a single shack being pulled down, while the longer one and the Colored American referred to shacks or houses.
Afterward the twenty, described as the entire Black population of Webrum, gathered their belongings, went to the railroad station and boarded a freight train for Vintondale, a nearby station.
No report of Aiken's capture, of any arrest among the white residents, of injuries, or of the Black residents' return appears in the coverage.

The short dispatch ran on February 24 in afternoon papers including the Topeka State Journal under the headline "Driven Out," the Minneapolis Journal as "Shacks Pulled Down," and the Washington Evening Star, whose subhead said Webrum citizens were "Perjudiced Because of Shooting Affray." The next day it appeared in the Wheeling Register as "Whites Razed Shack to the Ground," in the Omaha Daily Bee as "Shooting Starts Race War," and in the New-York Tribune under the ironic heading "Pennsylvania Also Loves Negro." Printings varied in detail: the Richmond Times-Dispatch and the Raleigh News and Observer said Thomas had been killed, and the Hickman Courier in Kentucky gave the number driven out as "about 200."

Southern papers made the episode a sectional point. The News and Observer headed it "Yankees Run the Negroes Out," the Keowee Courier of South Carolina "How It's Done In Pennsylvania," and the Lancaster Ledger, which misplaced Webrum in Indiana under an "Indianapolis" dateline, added "An Occurrence That Never Happens in the South." The Weekly Iberian of New Iberia, Louisiana, quoted the longer dispatch in an editorial titled "Lo, the Poor Negro!" which argued that the Black man's lot in the North was "even more onerous and galling than it is in the South." A Texas weekly closed its two-sentence item with "This in Pennsylvania."

Through March a one-sentence paragraph credited to The Commoner, ending "Mississippi? No, Pennsylvania," passed through papers in Kentucky and New Hampshire, and the Staunton Spectator ran its own version ending "In the South? No. Pennsylvania." A Wilmington, North Carolina, exchange column reprinted the Staunton line beside a Newport News Press comment asking whether "our strenuous president" could punish "the lawless people of Webrum."

In the Black press the episode appeared as a single sentence in the Race Gleanings column of the Colored American of Washington on March 7. Without further comment, it reported that "twenty souls" had been driven out and their houses destroyed over "the shooting one day last week of a white loafer by a Negro," a description of the wounded man that appears in none of the white printings.

Most printings of the dispatch, including the longer version, said Aiken shot and wounded Thomas, while the Richmond Times-Dispatch printed that he "shot and killed" him. The white papers called Thomas a bookkeeper, and the Colored American called the man shot "a white loafer."

reader.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Webrum, Pennsylvania
bases: White residents ordered all the Black residents of Webrum to leave, pulled down their shacks with ropes and poles, and the whole Black population, about twenty, left by freight train (A1, A14, A17).

Every white report traces to one Indiana, Pa., dispatch of Feb. 24 in a short and a longer version (A1, A14), and the Colored American's brief (A17) gives no independent detail beyond its characterization of the wounded man, so no independent second account was found.

accounts.label: Short wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Ten days after Aiken shot and wounded Thomas and escaped, Webrum residents ordered the town's twenty or so Black residents out; when they did not go, white residents pulled down their shack with ropes and poles and they left by freight for Vintondale.

accounts.label: Longer wire dispatch
accounts.gist: A white mob armed with ropes and poles marched on the Black quarters, rigged tackle on the shacks and wrecked them after the residents ignored several days' notice; it called this the end of a 'race war' begun ten days earlier.

accounts.label: Black weekly's brief
accounts.gist: Twenty Black residents were driven out of Webrum by the whites and their houses destroyed over the shooting 'of a white loafer by a Negro'.

framing.detail: Northern and Midwestern papers ran the short dispatch under descriptive headlines such as 'Driven Out' and 'Whites Razed Shack to the Ground'.

Southern papers used the dispatch for sectional point-scoring: the Weekly Iberian's editorial 'Lo, the Poor Negro!' and the Keowee Courier's 'How It's Done In Pennsylvania', criticizing the North rather than defending or condemning the mob as such.
March paragraphs, one credited to The Commoner, framed it as 'Mississippi? No, Pennsylvania', and a Newport News Press comment called the townspeople 'the lawless people of Webrum'.
The Colored American ran a one-sentence item in its Race Gleanings column without comment, but called the man who was shot 'a white loafer'.

conflicts.note: Most printings of the same dispatch, including the longer version, say 'wounded'; the 'killed' wording appears in the Richmond printing (and a Raleigh reprint, A9).
The Black weekly's wording is a characterization not found in any white printing.
